paragraphs: In the preceding papers, my fellow citizens, I have tried to set before you, in a clear and convincing light, the importance of the Union to your political safety and happiness. I have laid out for you a tangle of dangers to which you would be exposed if you allowed the sacred knot that binds the people of America together to be cut or dissolved by ambition or avarice, by jealousy or misrepresentation. In the rest of the inquiry through which I propose to accompany you, the truths I mean to impress on you will receive further confirmation from facts and arguments not yet noticed. The road you still have to travel may in places seem tedious or irksome. If so, remember that you are in search of information on the most momentous subject that can occupy the attention of a free people; that the field you must cross is in itself spacious; and that the difficulties of the journey have been needlessly increased by the mazes with which sophistry has beset the way. My aim will be to clear the obstacles from your path as briefly as can be done without sacrificing usefulness to speed.

In keeping with the plan I have laid down for discussing the subject, the next point to be examined is the "insufficiency of the present Confederation to the preservation of the Union." It may perhaps be asked what need there is of reasoning or proof to illustrate a position that is neither disputed nor doubted, that the understanding and feelings of all classes of men accept, and that the opponents of the new Constitution admit in substance as readily as its friends. It must truly be acknowledged that, however they may differ in other respects, they generally seem to agree in this view at least: that there are serious imperfections in our national system, and that something must be done to rescue us from impending anarchy. The facts that support this opinion are no longer matters of speculation. They have forced themselves on the feelings of the people at large. They have at length wrung a reluctant confession of the reality of these defects in the scheme of our federal government from those whose mistaken policy has had the principal share in bringing us to the extremity we have reached, defects which the intelligent friends of the Union have long pointed out and regretted.

We may indeed fairly be said to have reached almost the last stage of national humiliation. There is scarcely anything that can wound the pride or degrade the character of an independent nation that we do not experience. Are there engagements which we are bound to keep by every tie that men respect? These are the subject of constant and unblushing violation. Do we owe debts to foreigners and to our own citizens, contracted in a time of imminent peril for the preservation of our political existence? These remain without any proper or satisfactory provision for their payment. Are valuable territories and important posts held by a foreign power which, by express stipulations, ought long since to have been surrendered? They are still retained, to the harm of our interests no less than of our rights. Are we in a condition to resent or repel the aggression? We have neither troops, nor treasury, nor government.(1) Are we even in a condition to remonstrate with dignity? The just charges against our own good faith under the same treaty must first be removed. Are we entitled by nature and by compact to a free share in the navigation of the Mississippi? Spain shuts us out of it. Is public credit an indispensable resource in time of public danger? We seem to have given up its cause as desperate and hopeless. Is commerce important to national wealth? Ours is at its lowest point of decline. Is respectability in the eyes of foreign powers a safeguard against foreign encroachments? The impotence of our government even keeps them from treating with us. Our ambassadors abroad are the mere pageants of a mock sovereignty. Is a violent and unnatural fall in the value of land a symptom of national distress? The price of improved land in most parts of the country is much lower than the quantity of wasteland on the market can account for. It can be fully explained only by the lack of private and public confidence, which is alarmingly widespread among all ranks and which tends directly to depress the value of property of every kind. Is private credit the friend and patron of industry? The most useful kind, which concerns borrowing and lending, is reduced within the narrowest limits, and this is due still more to a feeling of insecurity than to a scarcity of money. To shorten a list of particulars that can afford neither pleasure nor instruction, we may ask in general: what sign of national disorder, poverty, and insignificance could befall a community so especially blessed with natural advantages as ours that is not already part of the dark catalogue of our public misfortunes?

This is the melancholy situation to which we have been brought by the very maxims and counsels that would now deter us from adopting the proposed Constitution. Not content with having led us to the brink of a precipice, they seem determined to plunge us into the abyss that awaits us below. Here, my countrymen, driven by every motive that ought to influence an enlightened people, let us make a firm stand for our safety, our tranquillity, our dignity, our reputation. Let us at last break the fatal charm that has too long lured us away from the paths of happiness and prosperity.

It is true, as has been observed before, that facts too stubborn to be resisted have produced a kind of general agreement with the abstract proposition that there are serious defects in our national system. But the usefulness of this concession by the old adversaries of federal measures is destroyed by their strenuous opposition to a remedy, on the only principles that can give it a chance of success. While they admit that the government of the United States has no energy, they argue against giving it the powers needed to supply that energy. They still seem to aim at things that are contradictory and irreconcilable: at an increase of federal authority without a decrease of State authority; at sovereignty in the Union and complete independence in its members. They still, in short, seem to cherish with blind devotion the political monster of an imperium in imperio. This makes it necessary to display fully the principal defects of the Confederation, in order to show that the evils we experience do not come from minor or partial imperfections. They come from fundamental errors in the structure of the building, which cannot be corrected except by altering the first principles and main pillars of the fabric.

The great and radical vice in the construction of the existing Confederation is the principle of LEGISLATION for STATES or GOVERNMENTS, in their CORPORATE or COLLECTIVE CAPACITIES, as distinguished from the INDIVIDUALS of which they consist. This principle does not run through all the powers delegated to the Union, yet it pervades and governs those on which the effectiveness of the rest depends. Except as to the rule of appointment, the United States has unlimited discretion to make requisitions, or formal requests, for men and money. But it has no authority to raise either by regulations reaching the individual citizens of America. The consequence is that, although in theory the resolutions of the United States on these subjects are laws, constitutionally binding on the members of the Union, in practice they are mere recommendations, which the States observe or disregard at their option.

It is a singular instance of the capriciousness of the human mind that, after all the warnings experience has given us on this point, there should still be men who object to the new Constitution for departing from a principle that has been found the bane of the old one. That principle is in itself plainly incompatible with the idea of GOVERNMENT. It is a principle which, if it is to be carried out at all, must substitute the violent and bloody agency of the sword for the mild influence of the civil authority.

There is nothing absurd or impracticable in the idea of a league or alliance between independent nations for certain defined purposes, precisely stated in a treaty that regulates all the details of time, place, circumstance, and quantity, leaves nothing to future discretion, and depends for its execution on the good faith of the parties. Compacts of this kind exist among all civilized nations, subject to the usual ups and downs of peace and war, of observance and non-observance, as the interests or passions of the contracting powers dictate. In the early part of the present century there was an epidemic rage in Europe for this kind of compact, from which the politicians of the time fondly hoped for benefits that were never realized. To establish the balance of power and the peace of that part of the world, all the resources of negotiation were exhausted, and triple and quadruple alliances were formed. But they were scarcely formed before they were broken. They gave mankind an instructive but painful lesson in how little dependence can be placed on treaties that have no sanction beyond the obligations of good faith, and that set general considerations of peace and justice against the impulse of any immediate interest or passion.

If the individual States of this country are disposed to stand in a similar relation to each other, and to drop the project of a general DISCRETIONARY SUPERINTENDENCE, the scheme would indeed be harmful and would bring upon us all the harms that were listed under the first head. But it would have the merit of being at least consistent and practicable. Abandoning all views toward a confederate government, it would bring us to a simple alliance, offensive and defensive. It would put us in a situation to be alternately friends and enemies of each other, as our mutual jealousies and rivalries, nourished by the intrigues of foreign nations, should dictate.

But if we are unwilling to be placed in this perilous situation, and if we still adhere to the design of a national government, which is the same thing as a superintending power under the direction of a common council, we must resolve to build into our plan those ingredients that may be considered as forming the characteristic difference between a league and a government. We must extend the authority of the Union to the persons of the citizens, the only proper objects of government.

Government implies the power of making laws. It is essential to the idea of a law that it be attended with a sanction, in other words, a penalty or punishment for disobedience. If no penalty is attached to disobedience, the resolutions or commands that pretend to be laws will in fact amount to nothing more than advice or recommendation. This penalty, whatever it may be, can be inflicted in only two ways: by the agency of the courts and ministers of justice, or by military force; by the COERCION of the civil authority, or by the COERCION of arms. The first kind can evidently apply only to individual men; the last kind must of necessity be used against bodies politic, or communities, or States. It is evident that no process of a court can enforce the observance of the laws against them in the last resort. Sentences may be pronounced against them for violations of their duty, but these sentences can be carried into execution only by the sword. In an association where the general authority is confined to the collective bodies of the communities that compose it, every breach of the laws must involve a state of war, and military execution must become the only instrument of civil obedience. Such a state of things certainly cannot deserve the name of government, and no prudent man would choose to entrust his happiness to it.

There was a time when we were told that breaches by the States of the regulations of the federal authority were not to be expected; that a sense of common interest would govern the conduct of the individual members and would bring about full compliance with all the constitutional requisitions of the Union. This language, at the present day, would seem as wild as a great part of what we now hear from the same quarter will be thought when we have received further lessons from that best oracle of wisdom, experience. It betrayed at all times an ignorance of the true springs by which human conduct is moved, and it contradicted the original reasons for establishing civil power. Why has government been instituted at all? Because the passions of men will not follow the dictates of reason and justice without constraint. Has it been found that bodies of men act with more rectitude or greater disinterestedness than individuals? All careful observers of the conduct of mankind have inferred the contrary, and the inference rests on obvious reasons. Regard for reputation has a less active influence when the infamy of a bad action is to be divided among a number than when it falls on one person alone. A spirit of faction, which tends to mix its poison into the deliberations of all bodies of men, will often carry the persons who compose them into improprieties and excesses for which they would blush in a private capacity.

In addition to all this, there is in the nature of sovereign power an impatience of control. It disposes those invested with it to look with an evil eye on all outside attempts to restrain or direct its operations. From this spirit it happens that in every political association formed on the principle of uniting a number of lesser sovereignties in a common interest, there will be found a kind of eccentric tendency in the subordinate or inferior orbs, by which each makes a perpetual effort to fly off from the common center. This tendency is not hard to account for. It has its origin in the love of power. Power that is controlled or limited is almost always the rival and enemy of the power that controls or limits it. This simple proposition will teach us how little reason there is to expect that the persons entrusted with the administration of the affairs of the individual members of a confederacy will at all times be ready, with perfect good humor and an unbiased regard for the public welfare, to carry out the resolutions or decrees of the general authority. The reverse follows from the make-up of human nature.

If, therefore, the measures of the Confederacy cannot be carried out without the intervention of the particular administrations, there will be little prospect of their being carried out at all. The rulers of the individual members, whether they have a constitutional right to or not, will undertake to judge the propriety of the measures themselves. They will consider whether the thing proposed or required fits their immediate interests or aims, and what momentary conveniences or problems would attend its adoption. All this will be done in a spirit of interested and suspicious scrutiny, without the knowledge of national circumstances and reasons of state that is essential to a right judgment, and with a strong preference for local objects that can hardly fail to mislead the decision. The same process must be repeated in every member of which the body is made up. The carrying out of plans framed by the councils of the whole will always depend on the discretion of the ill-informed and prejudiced opinion of every part. Those who have had experience of the proceedings of popular assemblies have seen how difficult it often is, where there is no outside pressure of circumstances, to bring them to harmonious resolutions on important points. They will readily see how impossible it must be to induce a number of such assemblies, deliberating at a distance from each other, at different times, and under different impressions, to cooperate for long in the same views and pursuits.

In our case, the concurrence of thirteen distinct sovereign wills is required under the Confederation for the complete execution of every important measure that proceeds from the Union. It has turned out as might have been foreseen. The measures of the Union have not been carried out. The delinquencies of the States have, step by step, matured to an extreme that has at length brought all the wheels of the national government to a dreadful standstill. Congress at this time scarcely has the means of keeping up the forms of administration until the States can find time to agree on a more substantial replacement for the present shadow of a federal government. Things did not come to this desperate extreme all at once. The causes I have named at first produced only unequal and disproportionate degrees of compliance with the requisitions of the Union. The greater deficiencies of some States gave the complying States, or the least delinquent, the pretext of an example and the temptation of self-interest. Why should we do more in proportion than those who are embarked with us on the same political voyage? Why should we agree to bear more than our proper share of the common burden? These were suggestions that human selfishness could not withstand, and that even speculative men, who looked ahead to remote consequences, could not combat without hesitation. Each State, yielding to the persuasive voice of immediate interest or convenience, has successively withdrawn its support, until the frail and tottering edifice seems ready to fall on our heads and crush us beneath its ruins.
